analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments, wiping out federal air pollution controls added that year.
analysis.headline: Rep. Tom DeLay's bill to repeal the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing, and died in committee when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill was a single sentence repealing Public Law 101-549, the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 [S3]. Those amendments are the law behind the acid rain program that cuts sulfur dioxide from power plants, tighter smog and soot standards, cleaner gasoline, and controls on toxic air pollutants. Repealing them would have erased those requirements. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on October 6, 1994 and received no further action before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been coal-fired power plants, refiners, automakers, and chemical manufacturers, which would have been freed from the emissions controls, cleaner-fuel mandates, and toxic pollution limits the 1990 amendments imposed. Some electricity consumers might have seen somewhat lower rates in the short run, since utilities would no longer have carried compliance costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Public Law 101-549 in its entirety [S3]. For industries regulated under the 1990 amendments — power plants subject to the acid rain program, refiners required to make cleaner gasoline, automakers facing tighter tailpipe limits — repeal would have ended those obligations and their compliance costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people would have paid with dirtier air: more acid rain, more smog and soot, more toxic air pollution, and the public health costs that follow — asthma, respiratory illness, and environmental damage. The costs of pollution would have shifted from the industries that produce it to the public that breathes it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone breathing the resulting dirtier air

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have erased the acid rain program and other pollution controls created by the 1990 amendments, returning utilities, refiners, and automakers to the weaker pre-1990 rules and shifting the resulting pollution onto the public [S2].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the 1990 amendments impose real, multi-billion-dollar compliance costs on power plants, refiners, and other industries — costs that show up partly in electricity and fuel prices — and repeal was pitched as removing that burden. The trade-off is that those costs buy measurable reductions in acid rain, smog, and toxic air pollution.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings would have gone almost entirely to a concentrated set of polluting industries, while the costs — dirtier air, more acid rain, more toxic emissions, and the associated health damage — would have spread across the entire public. The bill was also a one-line full repeal with no attempt to replace the 1990 rules with anything else, so there was no narrower design to weigh against the loss of the pollution controls.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom DeLay introduced the bill on October 6, 1994 [S1].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill's only action after referral was its death at the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the 1990 clean air standards stayed in force, so the public kept the pollution protections the bill would have erased. No industry gained anything, since nothing changed in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept its clean air rules

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990 and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never scheduled the bill for any action.

sides.party_line_note: There is no record of any vote or floor debate; the only sign of support was the sponsor himself, with zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: The 1990 amendments created the acid rain program requiring utilities to cut sulfur dioxide emissions. Repeal would have freed coal plants from those costs while returning the resulting acid rain to the public [S2].
The 1990 amendments mandated cleaner-burning gasoline, including reformulated fuel in smoggy areas. Repeal would have ended those requirements, cutting refiners' costs at the price of more smog [S2].
The 1990 amendments tightened tailpipe emission limits. Repeal would have rolled those standards back to pre-1990 levels [S2].
The 1990 amendments added controls on toxic air pollutants from industrial sources. Repeal would have lifted those limits [S2].
